text: In a Civilian Conservation Corps camp, the day began with reveille at six in the morning.
Then came showers, calisthenics and breakfast, and the flag went up before the men left for work.
At eight, the crews were handed over to National Park Service rangers. They worked until five, with an hour for lunch.
Dinner was at six, and lights were out at ten. Weeknight evenings meant classes and sports, and weekends were free.
These pictures show Utah camps at Milford. The schedule comes from the National Park Service account of the camps at Zion.
Thirty dollars a month. That was the pay for a young man in the Civilian Conservation Corps.
Twenty-five of those dollars were sent automatically to his family back home.
The men were single, and between eighteen and twenty-five at first. The age range was later widened to seventeen through twenty-eight.
A term lasted six months, and a company held about two hundred men.
The average member had finished only eight or nine grades of school, so many used camp classes to improve their reading and writing, or to learn a trade.
At Zion, Civilian Conservation Corps crews sloped the banks and built retaining walls for the switchbacks below the Zion–Mount Carmel Tunnel, including the Nevada Switchback.
Much of the work was done by hand, in a forty-hour week. That kept costs down, and made sure there was enough work to go around.
The corps was sometimes called Roosevelt's Tree Army, because its crews were so often sent to plant trees.
These desert bighorn sheep live in Zion today. But by the middle of the twentieth century, they were gone from the park.
Desert bighorn have roamed the Southwest for at least twelve thousand years, and their numbers may once have reached the millions.
Human encroachment, hunting, lost habitat and disease from domestic livestock all took their toll.
The National Park Service and Utah wildlife officials restored fourteen sheep to Zion by nineteen seventy-eight. At first, the effort did not appear to be working.
Fourteen sheep. That is how many had been restored to Zion by nineteen seventy-eight.
By twenty eighteen, the herd had grown to more than five hundred animals.
The secret is the rock. Bighorn favor steep, rocky ground, which helps them escape predators like mountain lions.
In spring, they can go many days without drinking, getting their moisture from plants. In dry periods, they visit water-filled potholes and springs.
Now biologists are concerned the herd may be too dense, because contact with domestic sheep or goats could spread diseases that are fatal to wild bighorn.
Twelve pounds. That is how much weight Civilian Conservation Corps men commonly gained in their first two months at camp.
They ate three meals a day, usually eggs for breakfast, sandwiches for lunch, and meat and vegetables for dinner. Zion's canyon camps even had their own bakers.
Every summer, from July through October, bighorn rams clash horns, and the dominant male gains access to the ewes.
Lambs are born about six months later. At Zion, newborns can be seen from mid-January through April.
